title: Async arrival load harness for mixed-workload continuous-batching evaluation
creator: Priya Desai
description:
Goal: Build a reproducible load/test harness that isolates continuous-batching + queueing interactions under realistic mixed workloads and produces stable tokens/sec and tail-latency (p95/p99) signals for regression detection. Motivation: recent production incidents showed p95 latency spikes when short interactive requests mix with long generation requests. We need a lab-grade driver that can emulate arrival distributions, request mixes, and KV cache reuse patterns to measure how batching and queueing policies affect token throughput and tail latency.

Success criteria:
- Harness can reproduce baseline stable tokens/sec and p95 values within +/-5% across repeated runs.
- Generates dashboards with per-route p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, batch size distribution, queue length over time, and percent of requests routed to fallback models.
- CI job that runs a focused regression suite and raises an alert (GitHub PR check) if p95 latency regresses by >15% or tokens/sec drops by >10% compared to baseline.

Design summary:
- Driver: loader-sim (Go) that supports configurable arrival processes (Poisson, bursty Pareto bursts, time-varying diurnal), request mixes (short chat turns, medium completions, long streaming generations, embeddings), and per-connection KV cache warmness options.
- Test cluster: small dedicated test pool on Dedicated infra (2x A100 or equivalent) with pinned model version. Avoids noisy shared hosted capacity.
- Metrics: tokens/sec, request/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency (generation-only and end-to-end), batch size histogram, queue length, observed KV cache hit ratio, and kernel utilization. Export to Prometheus/Grafana.
- Experiment matrix: vary offered load (0.2x to 1.5x of estimated capacity), mix ratios (0/100, 30/70, 70/30 short:long), arrival skew, and scheduling configs (max_batch_ms, max_batch_tokens, priority preemption).
- Analysis: run N=10 repeats per cell, compute median and 95% CI for tokens/sec and p95. Use bootstrap to detect regressions vs baseline. Provide automatic KS or Mann-Whitney tests for distribution shifts on latency tails.

Automation and integration:
- Baseline snapshots stored in bench-artifacts bucket with labels for runtime, kernel build, and model sha.
- A GitHub Actions workflow that runs a small smoke harness on PRs touching runtime or scheduler code. A full regression runs nightly and stores results in the bench dashboard.

Deliverables:
- loader-sim repo dir: github.com/redwood-inference/loader-sim (driver + YAML experiment spec).
- Grafana dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/bench/continuous-batching-mixed-workloads
- CI hooks: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/.github/workflows/bench.yml#L1-L120
- Runbook describing how to interpret slope charts and how to rebaseline after kernel upgrades.

Constraints and risks:
- Requires short windows of dedicated GPU access — coordinate with infra reservations team.
- Some noise remains due to non-deterministic kernel scheduling; mitigations include isolating NUMA and repeating runs.

Next steps:
1) Land initial loader-sim prototype and simple Poisson short+long mixed workload test (owner: Owen).
2) Add metric exports and dashboard panels (owner: Observability team).
3) Create PR-level smoke check and nightly full regression job.

Notes: keep the harness flexible to support both hosted and Dedicated topologies later.
